## 2.0 Nonlinear effects

- In physics, a function is nonlinear if the outcome (*y*) is not simply the additive product of all of the causes (*x*'s)
  - This can happen because effects of continuous IVs are not constant
  - This can happen because some effects are contingent upon values of other IVs
- In applied statistics, we usually distinguish between those two sources:
  - When **effects of an IV are not constant we say the effect is nonlinear**
    - E.g., The prediction line is not perfectly straight
  - When **the effect of one IV is contingent on the effects of another IV**, we say the effects are **interactive** (as opposed to additive)
- Note everything above is in terms of ***effects***. Linear regression **models** can---and often do---produce **nonlinear effects**. They often produce **interactive effects**. They can even produce **nonlinear interactive effects**
- Linear regression coefficients are useful when the effects are linear and additive. But this is a very special case. When effects are nonlinear and/or interactive we need different methods of summarizing and interpreting effects

## 2.10 Conclusion

- Do not assume a linear regression **model** is restricted to linear **effects**
- Useful to distinguish between linear and nonlinear effects
  - And between additive and interactive effects
- Linear regression models can produce nonlinear and/or interactive effects
- All models for categorical DVs produce nonlinear and interactive effects
  - Tools for interpretation are largely the same as we covered in this section:
    - Predictions
    - Visualizations
    - Marginal effects
